title: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers
summary: Defines and discusses the requirements for devices that forward packets at the network layer of the Internet protocol suite, meaning IPv4 routers. It is a standards-track specification covering forwarding behavior and related protocols.

eli5.summary: A rulebook for the machines that pass Internet packages along, explaining what they must do to be good citizens.

questions: what are the requirements for an ipv4 router
how should an ip router forward packets
how does a router choose the next hop
should a router forward directed broadcasts
what is router compliance in rfc 1812
subtitle: The rulebook for what a device must do to forward IPv4 packets, with the corrections and advice that vendors needed.

tldr.problem: Routers from different vendors had to interoperate across the growing Internet, but the rules were scattered across many protocol documents, and past implementations had repeatedly made the wrong choice.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1812 walks through IP, ICMP, IGMP, forwarding, routing protocols, management and operations, restating requirements with MUST, SHOULD and MAY, correcting errors in the referenced documents and adding guidance.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1716 and RFC 1009 as the router requirements document, and has since been updated by RFC 2644 and RFC 6633.

today: RFC 1812 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1009 and RFC 1716, and it has been updated by RFC 2644 and RFC 6633. It has not been obsoleted. It covers IP version 4 only.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope of the Memo
sections.content:
RFC 1812 defines requirements for devices that perform the network layer forwarding function of the Internet protocol suite. The text notes that the Internet community calls them IP routers or simply routers, the OSI community calls them intermediate systems, and older documents called them gateways.

A router is distinguished from other packet switching devices because it examines the IP header while switching. It generally removes the Link Layer header the message arrived with, modifies the IP header, and puts on a new Link Layer header for retransmission.

The memo replaces RFC 1716 and covers only TCP/IP, even though many routers support other protocol suites. It lists standard protocols a router must use and incorporates the current specifications by reference. It also corrects errors in those documents and adds guidance for implementors. The authors say the list of requirements is incomplete by itself: the full set is mostly in the protocol specifications, with this memo's corrections and additions.

It should be read together with the host requirements documents, RFC 1122 and RFC 1123. The main difference between hosts and routers is that routers implement forwarding algorithms. Any host acting as a router must follow this memo.

The memo admits that most implementations of the time failed to meet its requirements in minor or major ways. It describes the specification as the ideal towards which the Internet needs to move.
sections.eli5: This is a big rulebook for the machines that pass Internet packages along. It says what they must do, and it fixes mistakes that earlier rulebooks made.

sections.title: Reading the Requirements and Compliance
sections.content:
The memo uses capitalized words to rate each requirement: MUST, MUST IMPLEMENT, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD IMPLEMENT, SHOULD NOT and MAY. The MUST IMPLEMENT phrase means the item has to be built in, but need not be enabled by default.

Each major chapter has an introduction, a protocol walk-through that goes through the protocol documents section by section, and a specific issues part for matters the walk-through did not cover. Paragraphs labeled DISCUSSION or IMPLEMENTATION explain and suggest, and are not part of the standard.

Compliance only counts the requirements relevant to the features and protocols a router actually implements. An implementation that fails any relevant MUST, MUST IMPLEMENT or MUST NOT is not compliant.

A router may offer an option that violates a MUST, but only if that option's default setting conforms to the memo. The authors strongly recommend against providing such options. They also call the memo closer to a profile than a full specification, because most protocol content is not repeated and implementors must still follow the underlying specifications.

Algorithms in the memo are described for clarity. A router need not implement them literally, but its behavior toward the outside world must match a strict, literal implementation.
sections.eli5: The rulebook uses special words for how strict each rule is. 'MUST' is a rule you cannot skip, 'SHOULD' is a strong hint, and 'MAY' is up to you.

sections.title: How the Internet Sees a Router
sections.content:
Chapter 2 contains no requirements, only background. It lists what an Internet router does: it follows IP, ICMP and other required protocols; connects to two or more packet networks and handles each network's framing, MTU and address translation; receives and forwards datagrams while dealing with buffers, congestion and fairness; chooses a next hop from its routing database; usually runs an interior gateway protocol and sometimes an exterior one; and provides management and support facilities.

The memo states the architectural assumptions routers rely on. The Internet is a network of networks. Routers keep no connection state: each packet is forwarded independently, which lets redundant paths survive failures, and end-to-end flow control and reliability live in the hosts. Routing complexity belongs in the routers, not the hosts. And the system must tolerate wide variation in bandwidth, delay, loss, reordering and packet size.

The text also explains addressing. Classical Class A to E prefixes and subnets are now described as historical. CIDR replaces them with arbitrary-length network prefixes, built on topologically significant address assignment, routing protocols that aggregate reachability information, and a consistent longest-match forwarding algorithm. Routers SHOULD always treat a route as a network prefix.

It adds that future developments may put more state into routers, naming multicast routing, resource reservation and flow based forwarding as likely examples.
sections.eli5: A router is a town crossing that knows several roads. It looks at each package's address, picks the next road, and does not remember the package afterwards.

sections.title: IP Handling and the Forwarding Steps
sections.content:
Routers MUST implement IP, plus subnets, IP broadcast and CIDR. Before a router acts on any packet it MUST validate the header. A packet is silently discarded, and the error SHOULD be logged, if the Link Layer length is under the 20-byte minimum, the checksum is wrong, the version is not 4, the header length field is under 5 words, or the total length cannot hold the header. A router MUST NOT have an option to disable these checks, and MUST NOT provide a way to disable checksum verification.

The general forwarding procedure is: receive the packet, validate the header, process most options, then decide among three cases. The packet is for the router itself, or it is queued for forwarding, or it is forwarded and also delivered locally. For unicast the forwarder finds the next hop, checks that forwarding is permitted, decrements the TTL by at least one, finishes option processing, fragments if needed, finds the next hop's Link Layer address, encapsulates the packet and sends it, and sends an ICMP redirect if necessary.

Time to Live. A router MUST NOT check the TTL of a packet except when forwarding it. When forwarding it MUST reduce the TTL by at least one. If the TTL reaches zero the packet MUST be discarded, and for non-multicast destinations the router MUST send ICMP Time Exceeded code 0. The memo says Time Exceeded is required because traceroute depends on it.

Fragmentation. A router MUST support fragmentation, SHOULD minimize the number of fragments, and MUST NOT reassemble a transit datagram before forwarding it, because fragments may take different paths. Routers do reassemble datagrams addressed to themselves.

Reserved header bits MUST be ignored and passed through unchanged, so future IP revisions can use them without upgrading every router. Unrecognized IP options MUST be ignored and passed through unchanged.
sections.eli5: A router first checks that the package label is readable and sane. Then it lowers a countdown number on the label. If the countdown hits zero, it throws the package away and sends a note back.

sections.title: Choosing the Next Hop
sections.content:
To decide where to send a packet, a router first asks whether the destination is directly reachable by comparing network prefixes of its interfaces (and router-ids for unnumbered links). If not, it consults its Forwarding Information Base (FIB) and applies pruning rules in order, each discarding candidate routes until normally one remains.

The required rules are Basic Match, Longest Match, Weak TOS (applied only if the router considers TOS), Best Metric and Vendor Policy. For example, for a destination of 10.144.2.5 with prefixes 10.144.2.0/24, 10.144.0.0/16 and 10.0.0.0/8, Longest Match keeps only the /24. Preference runs from host routes, through network prefix routes of decreasing length, down to the default route, which is the route with prefix length zero.

If no route is left, the packet MUST be discarded and an appropriate ICMP error generated. If several routes remain, the router may pick one arbitrarily or use load-splitting. The memo notes that a wise implementor who offers load-splitting will let the network manager disable it.

One suggested Vendor Policy is administrative preference, an integer from 0 (most preferred) to 254 (least preferred), with 255 meaning the route must never be used. The text warns that it is not safe, since it can easily be misused to create routing loops. Appendix E covers additional pruning rules and the algorithms used by OSPF and Integrated IS-IS.
sections.eli5: The router has a list of possible roads. It crosses off the ones that do not lead to the address, then picks the road that matches the address most closely.

sections.title: ICMP Errors and When Not to Send Them
sections.content:
ICMP reports forwarding problems. The memo tells routers which messages to send, and just as importantly when to stay quiet. An ICMP error MUST NOT be sent in response to another ICMP error, a packet that fails header validation, a packet sent to an IP broadcast or multicast address or as a Link Layer broadcast or multicast, a packet with an invalid source address, or any fragment other than the first. These restrictions take precedence over every other requirement. They exist to prevent broadcast storms.

Routers MUST be able to generate Destination Unreachable and SHOULD pick the code that best matches the cause. The memo defines new codes 13, 14 and 15, and says Code 6 SHOULD NOT be generated. Routers SHOULD limit the rate of ICMP errors and the rate limit parameters SHOULD be configurable.

Redirects. Routers MUST NOT generate network redirects (codes 0 and 2) and only send host redirects, because subnets and CIDR make network redirects ambiguous. A redirect may only be sent when the packet leaves by the interface it arrived on, the source is on the same logical network as the next hop, and there is no source route option. A router running a routing protocol MUST NOT use paths learned from redirects.

Source Quench. A router SHOULD NOT originate Source Quench messages, since research suggests it consumes bandwidth but is an ineffective and unfair antidote to congestion.

Other required behaviors include an Echo server, responding to Address Mask Requests (with a configuration option that defaults to allowing responses), and support for the router side of ICMP Router Discovery. Information Request and Reply are obsolete and SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: When a router cannot deliver a package it can send a note saying why. But it must never send notes about notes, or notes about broadcasts, or everyone would be buried in notes.

sections.title: Routing Protocols and Route Filtering
sections.content:
The memo separates interior routing, within an autonomous system, from exterior routing between systems. A router that implements any routing protocol other than static routes MUST IMPLEMENT OSPF, specified in the memo's references as OSPF version 2. IS-IS adapted to IP (Dual or Integrated IS-IS) is also described. Among exterior protocols, EGP is called historical and BGP-4 is growing in popularity. A router is not required to implement any inter-AS protocol, but one that implements EGP MUST IMPLEMENT BGP. RIP and EGP are covered in an appendix of historical routing protocols.

Routing is described as one of the few places where the robustness principle does not apply. Routers should be suspicious of routing data. They SHOULD be able to rank information sources by trust, SHOULD filter obviously invalid routes such as those for net 127, MUST NOT by default redistribute routes they do not use or trust, and SHOULD set the IP precedence of routing traffic they originate to 6 (Internetwork Control).

Routers MUST support static routes and let each static route carry a metric for a given routing domain. They MUST be able to exchange routes between separate interior routing protocols, MUST provide a mechanism to avoid loops when doing so in both directions, and MUST provide a way to prioritize routes from independent routing processes.

Route filtering requirements include accepting routing information on chosen logical interfaces, and choosing whether all routes or only a default route is advertised on an interface.
sections.eli5: Routers gossip with each other about which roads lead where. The rules say to trust good neighbors more, to double-check strange gossip, and not to pass along rumors you do not believe.

sections.title: Management, Configuration and Operations
sections.content:
Routers MUST be manageable by SNMP over UDP/IP, and all SNMP operations (get, get-next, get-response, set and trap) MUST be implemented. Management requests must work when sent to any IP address on any of the router's interfaces. Routers MUST rate-limit SNMP traps. The community table MUST allow at least one entry and SHOULD allow at least two, and be saved in non-volatile storage. If it starts with a default entry, that entry SHOULD be named public, be read-only and MUST NOT send traps. The memo lists the standard MIBs a router MUST implement for the interfaces and protocols it has, such as the System, Interface, IP, ICMP and UDP groups of MIB-II. Vendor specific MIBs MUST expose everything not covered by the standard ones.

Operations requirements cover initialization and upkeep. A router MUST NOT enable forwarding on an interface until it knows an IP address and mask or prefix length for it, or knows it is unnumbered and knows its router-id. These MUST be explicitly configured and must not come from factory defaults, since shipped default addresses had been advertised into live networks. Routers MUST support out-of-band access, MUST allow in-band and out-of-band reload, and SHOULD be reconfigurable without a reboot. A router SHOULD NOT believe protocols such as RARP or ICMP Address Mask Reply for configuration.

Routers MUST provide in-band access, but for security it SHOULD be disabled by default, and the default must be documented. A router MUST be able to initiate an ICMP echo and SHOULD be able to initiate a traceroute.
sections.eli5: The people who run the network need to check on routers from far away. So routers must answer questions, accept settings only from the right people, and never come with secret built-in passwords.

sections.title: Filtering, Broadcasts and Security
sections.content:
The memo says its focus is interoperability rather than security, yet many of its rules affect security. Its security concerns are denial of service, integrity and authentication. It admits that few network protocols of the time had reasonable built-in security.

Address and source checks. A router SHOULD NOT forward packets with invalid source or destination addresses (often called martians), or with addresses on network 0 or network 127. A router SHOULD IMPLEMENT source address validation, discarding a packet whose arrival interface is not the one it would use to reach the source address, but this MUST be disabled by default because asymmetric paths can make it drop valid packets.

Broadcasts. Limited broadcasts MUST NOT be forwarded and MUST NOT be discarded. Network-prefix-directed broadcasts MUST be forwarded given a route and no policy, but a router MUST have an option to disable forwarding them, which defaults to permit. A router MUST NOT forward a packet it received as a Link Layer broadcast unless it is directed to an IP multicast address. All-subnets-directed broadcasts are called meaningless under CIDR.

Filtering and options. Routers SHOULD offer packet filtering by source and destination prefix, with silent discard or an ICMP code 13 reply. Source routing MUST be supported but may be disabled by an option that is not enabled by default. Record Route and Timestamp can reveal topology, so options to ignore them are allowed.

Auditing. Routers MUST provide a way to audit security failures and policy violations, limited or disabled on request, and MUST NOT have undocumented back doors or master passwords.
sections.eli5: Routers have to be careful guards. They ignore packages with fake or impossible return addresses, do not repeat shouts meant for one street, and keep a log when someone tries something sneaky.

viz.caption: THE NEXT-HOP PRUNING RULES, APPLIED IN ORDER (RFC 1812)

items.title: 1. Basic Match
items.text: Keep only routes whose prefix matches the destination address.

items.title: 2. Longest Match
items.text: Of those, keep the routes with the longest prefix length.

items.title: 3. Weak TOS
items.text: Prefer routes whose TOS equals the packet's, else default TOS 0000. Applies only if TOS is considered.

items.title: 4. Best Metric
items.text: Within one routing domain, drop routes with an inferior metric.

items.title: 5. Vendor Policy
items.text: A catch-all for vendor-specific choices, such as administrative preference.

viz.caption: ICMP DESTINATION UNREACHABLE CODES DISCUSSED IN RFC 1812

items.label: Network Unreachable
items.desc: No route to the destination network.

items.label: Host Unreachable
items.desc: No path to a host on a directly connected network.

items.label: Fragmentation Needed and DF Set
items.desc: Fragmentation required but the DF flag is set.

items.label: Source Route Failed
items.desc: Cannot reach the next hop in a source route option.

items.label: Destination Network Unknown
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be generated; use code 0 instead.

items.label: Network Unreachable for TOS
items.desc: Routes exist but none has an acceptable TOS.

items.label: Host Unreachable for TOS
items.desc: No route matches the requested or default TOS.

items.label: Precedence Cutoff in Effect
items.desc: Packet precedence is below the minimum required.
